title: Cosmetic Dentistry Cost: What Treatments Cost and Who Pays
h1: How Much Does Cosmetic Dentistry Cost, and Does Insurance Help?
description: Cosmetic dentistry costs vary widely by treatment. Why insurance rarely pays, how the 100-80-50 plan structure works, and how to budget for a smile makeover.
meta_keywords: cosmetic dentistry cost, cosmetic dental work cost, smile makeover cost, does insurance cover cosmetic dentistry
quick_answer: Cosmetic dentistry costs vary widely, from modest fees for whitening or bonding to thousands for veneers or full smile makeovers. Most cosmetic treatment is paid out of pocket because insurance usually covers only care that restores health or function. A typical plan pays 100% preventive, 80% basic and 50% major care up to an annual maximum, for example $1,500, according to Delta Dental.
key_takeaways: Cosmetic dentistry includes whitening, bonding, veneers, gum contouring and smile makeovers.
Costs range from modest single treatments to large multi-tooth plans.
Insurance usually excludes purely cosmetic treatment.
Treatment that also restores damage, like crowns, may be partly covered as major care at 50%.
Annual maximums, such as $1,500, limit what insurance pays each year.

sections.html:
Cosmetic dentistry is dental treatment whose main purpose is improving the appearance of the teeth, gums or smile. Common cosmetic treatments include teeth whitening, dental bonding, porcelain veneers, gum contouring, tooth reshaping and complete smile makeovers combining several procedures.

Some treatments are both cosmetic and restorative. A crown on a broken front tooth improves appearance and restores function, and clear aligners straighten teeth for both looks and bite. How a treatment is classified affects whether insurance contributes.

sections.h2: How much do cosmetic treatments cost?
sections.html:
Cosmetic treatment costs vary enormously depending on the procedure, the number of teeth and the dentist's experience. Whitening and small bonding repairs are at the lower end. Veneers on several teeth, smile makeovers and combinations of orthodontics, veneers and implants are at the upper end.

CareCredit's procedure cost list publishes national averages for many individual treatments, which is a useful starting point when planning. Because cosmetic results depend heavily on the skill of the dentist and lab, compare experience and before and after work as well as price.

Insurance usually does not cover cosmetic dentistry. Dental plans focus on preventing and treating disease and restoring function, so treatment done mainly for appearance, such as whitening or veneers on healthy teeth, is typically excluded.

When a treatment also addresses a health or functional problem, part of the cost may be covered. For example, a crown that restores a broken tooth is often covered as major care, which Delta Dental describes as typically paid at 50% on a 100-80-50 plan. See is dental insurance worth it for how plans work.

sections.h2: How does the annual maximum affect cosmetic plans?
sections.html:
The annual maximum limits how much insurance pays in a benefit year, which matters for large treatment plans. Delta Dental uses $1,500 as an example annual maximum in its annual maximum guide.

Even when parts of a smile makeover are covered, a multi-tooth plan can quickly reach the maximum, leaving the rest to you. Some people stage treatment across benefit years to use more than one maximum, when it is safe to do so.

sections.h2: Should restorative work come before cosmetic work?
sections.html:
Restorative work should usually come before cosmetic work. Cavities, gum disease, cracked teeth and failing fillings need to be treated first, because cosmetic restorations placed on unhealthy teeth or gums are less likely to last.

This also helps with costs, because restorative care is more likely to be covered by insurance. A good cosmetic plan often begins with a cleaning, any necessary fillings or gum treatment, and whitening, before any veneers or crowns are made.

sections.h2: What does a smile makeover involve?
sections.html:
A smile makeover is a personalised plan combining several cosmetic and restorative treatments to achieve an overall result. It might include whitening, orthodontic alignment, gum contouring, bonding or veneers on front teeth, and crowns or implants to replace damaged or missing teeth.

Planning usually involves photos, scans, models and sometimes a digital preview or trial smile. The total cost depends on how many teeth and treatments are involved. Ask for a written, itemised plan that shows which parts are cosmetic and which may be covered by insurance.

sections.h2: How can you pay for cosmetic dentistry?
sections.html:
You can pay for cosmetic dentistry through savings, in-house payment plans, medical credit or financing, and in some cases HSA or FSA funds for parts of treatment that are medically necessary. HSA and FSA rules usually exclude purely cosmetic procedures.

Some practices offer membership plans with discounts on cosmetic work. Read any financing terms carefully, including interest rates after promotional periods. See how much dental insurance costs if you are weighing a plan for the restorative parts of treatment.

sections.h2: How do you choose a cosmetic dentist?
sections.html:
Choosing a cosmetic dentist starts with their experience in the treatment you want. Ask to see before and after photos of their own cases, especially similar ones, and how long ago they were done.

Ask which dental lab they use, how they plan results, whether they offer previews, what follow-up is included and what happens if a restoration fails. A clear, itemised quote and honest discussion of limits and alternatives are good signs.

sections.h2: How can you reduce cosmetic dentistry costs?
sections.html:
You can reduce cosmetic dentistry costs by starting with the least invasive options. A professional cleaning and whitening may achieve much of what you want before considering veneers. Bonding can fix small chips and gaps at a lower cost than veneers.

Treating only the teeth that show when you smile, staging treatment over time, and using insurance for the restorative parts all help keep costs manageable.

sections.h2: How long do cosmetic results last?
sections.html:
How long cosmetic results last depends on the treatment. Whitening fades over months to years and needs touch-ups. Bonding may need repair or replacement after several years. Porcelain veneers and crowns can last many years with good care.

Budget for maintenance as well as the initial treatment, because most cosmetic work eventually needs refreshing.

sections.h2: Does straightening teeth count as cosmetic dentistry?
sections.html:
Straightening teeth with braces or clear aligners is often considered partly cosmetic and partly functional. Correcting crowding and bite problems makes teeth easier to clean and can reduce uneven wear, which is why many dental plans include orthodontic benefits, especially for children, though often with a separate lifetime maximum.

For adults, orthodontic coverage is less common. In smile makeovers, aligning teeth first can reduce the need for more invasive cosmetic work, such as veneers to mask crooked teeth, and can lead to a more conservative and longer-lasting result.

faq.q: How much does cosmetic dentistry cost?
faq.a: Cosmetic dentistry costs range from modest fees for whitening or small bonding repairs to thousands for veneers or full smile makeovers. The price depends on the treatment, number of teeth, materials and the dentist's experience. Ask for an itemised quote.

Insurance usually does not cover purely cosmetic dentistry such as whitening or veneers on healthy teeth. Treatments that also restore damage, such as crowns on broken teeth, may be partly covered as major care, often at 50%.

A smile makeover is a personalised combination of cosmetic and restorative treatments, such as whitening, orthodontics, bonding, veneers, crowns or implants, planned together to improve the overall appearance and function of your smile.

faq.q: How can I pay for cosmetic dental work?
faq.a: You can pay for cosmetic dental work with savings, in-house payment plans, medical financing or membership plans. HSA and FSA funds usually cannot be used for purely cosmetic treatment but may cover medically necessary parts.

faq.q: What is the cheapest cosmetic dental treatment?
faq.a: Professional cleaning, whitening and dental bonding are usually among the least expensive cosmetic treatments. They can make a noticeable difference before considering more costly options like veneers.
